blocks.text: **The task.** Given an unsorted array of integers, find the smallest **positive** integer that is absent. Required: O(N) time and O(1) space.
The bound that makes it possible
The array may contain anything — negatives, zeros, huge numbers. That sounds unbounded, but here is the key observation:
With N slots, the answer **must** lie in the range 1 to N+1. If the array happened to contain exactly 1 through N, the answer would be N+1. Any other case leaves a gap somewhere inside 1..N.
So every value outside 1..N is irrelevant and can be ignored. The range is bounded after all, and cyclic sort applies.
Each condition removes a specific failure:

items: **`nums[i] > 0`** — negatives and zero have no home; leave them where they fall.
**`nums[i] <= n`** — values beyond N have no slot; ignore them too.
**`nums[i] !== nums[target]`** — the target already holds this value, so swapping would spin forever on duplicates.

blocks.text: Same argument as plain cyclic sort: every swap permanently places one value, so swaps are capped at N. Junk values are skipped by a simple increment. Both loops together are O(N).
**Time: O(N)**, **Space: O(1)** — at the cost of rearranging the input.
This is considered a hard problem, and the difficulty is entirely in spotting that the answer is bounded by N+1. Once you see that, it is ordinary cyclic sort with careful guards.
